content.paragraph: We have looked at first-order differential equations from a geometric point of view (direction fields) and from a numerical point of view (Euler’s method). What about the symbolic point of view? It would be nice to have an explicit formula for a solution of a differential equation. Unfortunately, that is not always possible. But in this section we examine a certain type of differential equation that can be solved explicitly.

subsection.title: Orthogonal Trajectories
subsection.paragraph: An orthogonal trajectory of a family of curves is a curve that intersects each curve of the family orthogonally, that is, at right angles (see Figure 7). For instance, each member of the family $$y = mx$$ of straight lines through the origin is an orthogonal trajectory of the family $$x^{2} + y^{2} = r^{2}$$ of concentric circles with center the origin (see Figure 8). We say that the two families are orthogonal trajectories of each other.

figure.alt_text: “A family of 6 short consecutive concave down curves. A long concave down curve intersects each curve at right angles. The long curve is labeled as orthogonal trajectory.”

Three concentric circles and four orthogonal trajectory lines are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The circles are graphed with the origin as the center and all the lines pass through the origin. Each line intersects each circle at two points. Two lines enter the third quadrant and exit from the first quadrant. The other two lines enter the fourth quadrant and exit from the second quadrant.

subsection.paragraph: Orthogonal trajectories occur in various branches of physics. For example, in an electrostatic field the lines of force are orthogonal to the lines of constant potential. Also, the streamlines in aerodynamics are orthogonal trajectories of the velocity-equipotential curves.

subsection.title: Mixing Problems
subsection.paragraph: A typical mixing problem involves a tank of fixed capacity containing a thoroughly mixed solution of some substance, such as salt. A solution of a given concentration enters the tank at a fixed rate and the mixture, thoroughly stirred, leaves at a fixed rate, which may differ from the entering rate. If $$y(t)$$ denotes the amount of substance in the tank at time $$t$$ , then $$y^{\prime}(t)$$ is the rate at which the substance is being added minus the rate at which it is being removed. The mathematical description of this situation often leads to a first-order separable differential equation. We can use the same type of reasoning to model a variety of phenomena: chemical reactions, discharge of pollutants into a lake, injection of a drug into the bloodstream.

subsection.paragraph: If water (or other liquid) drains from a tank, we expect that the flow will be greatest at first (when the water depth is greatest) and will gradually decrease as the water level decreases. But we need a more precise mathematical description of how the flow decreases in order to answer the kinds of questions that engineers ask: How long does it take for a tank to drain completely? How much water should a tank hold in order to guarantee a certain minimum water pressure for a sprinkler system?

item.paragraph: In many parts of the world, the water for sprinkler systems in large hotels and hospitals is supplied by gravity from cylindrical tanks on or near the roofs of the buildings. Suppose such a tank has radius $$10$$ ft and the diameter of the outlet is $$2.5{inches}$$ . An engineer has to guarantee that the water pressure at the tank outlet will be at least $$2160{lb} \slash {ft}^{2}$$ for a period of $$10$$ minutes. (When a fire happens, the electrical system might fail and it could take up to $$10$$ minutes for the emergency generator and fire pump to be activated.) How tall should the engineer specify the tank to be in order to make such a guarantee? (Use the fact that the water pressure at a depth of $$d$$ feet is $$P = 62.5d{lb} \slash {ft}^{2}$$ .
